title: The Endurance of the Rocky Brand
text:
Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession. 

 Rocky has one of the best corny taglines Hollywood has ever cooked up. “His whole life was a million-to-one shot,” reads the poster ; below it is a stark black-and-white picture of the scrappy boxer Rocky Balboa (played by Sylvester Stallone) holding hands with his beloved Adrian (Talia Shire). Considering now, 50 years after the movie’s release, that this poster was doing its darndest to sell audiences on both a total unknown in Stallone and an outdated genre (the “boxing picture”) is hard. But it worked: Rocky was an out-of-nowhere smash, making more than $200 million globally on a $1 million budget and winning Best Picture at the frankly stacked 1977 Academy Awards.

 The movie succeeded partly because of how well it packaged that underdog narrative, both on-screen and off. Rocky is about a workaday schlub who is improbably selected for a title bout against the heavyweight champion, Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers). As he goes the distance in the ring, he wins the public’s adoration. But the discussion around the movie quickly coalesced around not its story, but its star. Stallone wrote the film and insisted, despite quite reasonable studio objections over his anonymity, that he play the lead role. His own dreams of triumph are coded into Rocky ’s DNA; it’s a gentle tale about the actor’s hope to make it big in Hollywood, transposed onto a boxer.

 All of this makes the existence of the new film I Play Rocky all the funnier. Directed by Peter Farrelly and starring the relatively unknown Anthony Ippolito as Stallone, it follows the making of Rocky ; the crux is Stallone’s bullheadedness about, well, playing Rocky. Seriously: The movie’s entire second act seems to involve various studio honchos calling him on the phone to offer more and more implausible amounts of money for him to be only the screenwriter, so that they can install some big star of the era (such as Ryan O’Neal and Burt Reynolds) in the title role instead. The most amusing moments see Tracy Letts as a (fictional) executive growing furious with the back-and-forth, befuddled that this no-name actor would dare turn down hundreds of thousands of dollars to just go away.

 Funnier still is that I Play Rocky really works, even though it’s basically an adaptation of various Wikipedia articles. The original Rocky already does a fine job exploring Stallone’s striving nature; here, we’re just watching an actor play another actor who’s dreaming big. But Ippolito does a great imitation, and the ensemble, which also includes P. J. Byrne (as the producer Irwin Winkler), Stephan James (as the cocksure Weathers), and Jay Duplass (as Rocky ’s director, John G. Avildsen), provide worthy support. One particularly charming sequence pays loving homage to the Steadicam, a then-recent invention that was used to great effect in Rocky ’s famous museum-steps sequence . The movie, overall, is an easy-to-enjoy ode to moviemaking.

 To me, though, it mostly illustrates the incredible endurance of the Rocky media brand. The franchise has produced nine entries total (if you include the three Creed films, as you must) and inspired many imitators. Almost every sequel, successful or not, figures out a way to bring our hero back down to earth so that he can be the underdog again: Rocky III acknowledges the character becoming a celebrity, while Rocky IV sees him becoming an anti-Soviet champion fighting on the world stage. Still, each iteration sweats to underline Stallone’s hangdog sweetness and shy, mumbling line delivery.

 As Stallone became world-famous, his other major franchise, Rambo (introduced in the 1980s once the actor was a cemented star), fully lost sight of what made its title character feel appealing and human, transforming a broken Vietnam veteran into a roided-up, bazooka-toting one-man slaughterhouse. Although the later Rocky movies certainly got cartoonish—the first entry practically feels like an art-house indie in comparison—the hero himself stayed pretty consistent. That’s why Stallone almost won an Oscar for playing the character as a slow-and-steady mentor in Creed 39 years later, and why Ippolito might get his own nod for imitating him. I Play Rocky portrays Stallone as bashful, devoted to his girlfriend and eventual first wife, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), and dismissed by everyone around him for seeming to have more brawn than brain. It’s a glossy fairy tale. But then, so is Rocky .

 An Essay I Enjoyed 

 Lionsgate 
 Hollywood’s Worst Tendencies, in One Movie

 By Shirley Li 

 Prequels for long-running franchises are tough to pull off. Too many Easter eggs, and the whole project comes across as hollow fan service. Too different from the other installments, and the new entry risks not making sense. But The Hunger Games had a lot of potential to mine new stories from its past. Panem, the totalitarian nation behind the titular battles royal, had a turbulent history filled with cinematic potential, as well as complicated characters whose lives could be further explored. And besides, the original tetralogy, based on Suzanne Collins’s popular YA books, made more than $3 billion at the box office worldwide.

 Coming Attractions 

 Now expanding in theaters is one of the year’s best debut films—heck, it’s one of the year’s best movies, period. The premise of Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid sounds unbelievably corny, recalling so many ’80s comedies—what if an inveterate party animal in New York’s club scene suddenly found out he was the father of a 10-year-old boy? But Firstman (who wrote, directed, and stars) has a precise sense of place and character, and manages to find a fresh and funny angle on a very schematic-sounding story by observing urban nightlife—and the necessary, healthy ego death that comes with raising a kid. Although Club Kid is mostly about how parenthood changes the adult, rather than the child, it is knowing about that level of self-involvement, and it lands its nuanced, very emotional ending.

 Also in theaters is La bola negra , a much-hyped epic that made a splashy debut at the Cannes Film Festival in May. It is Netflix’s big hope for the Oscars this year. The movie is a crowd-pleaser with an already vocal fan base, and I admired the scope of the co-directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s vision—yet I was left very frustrated by it. Summarizing everything that’s going on in the triptych of stories is tough, but La bola negra contains: a re-creation of a lost play by the poet Federico García Lorca; a tale of a young man in the Spanish Civil War who becomes a Nationalist in order to survive while nursing his love for a captive Republican soldier; and a section set in the near-present, where a character’s descendant delves into this history and whether it may have, in some way, inspired Lorca. I was most invested in the contemporary storyline and how it explores Spain’s oft-unspoken legacy of fascism. But I felt that the central plot, set in 1937, thematically bit off more than it could chew. Still, given the broad canvas it’s painting on, the movie is worth engaging with on the biggest screen available before it moves to streaming next week.

 What Else I’m Watching 

 Elsinore is another Oscar contender out now, and it’s worth seeing mostly for Andrew Scott’s lovely work in the lead role. He plays Ian Charleson, the Chariots of Fire actor who died of AIDS at the age of 40—right as he was starring as Hamlet at London’s National Theatre. Scott is tremendous, but the film is otherwise a little sloppily done, relying on formulaic inspirational-movie tropes I thought we’d disposed of long ago.

 I also caught up with the late Eleanor Coppola’s documentary Making Marie Antoinette , which is streaming on Mubi. It’s in the style of Hearts of Darkness , the film she shot about her husband Francis’s nightmarish time on the set of Apocalypse Now . This is obviously a more sentimental (and calmer) family portrait; Coppola captures her daughter, Sofia, as she works on Marie Antoinette , arguably her best movie. It’s quite sweet and wistful; Coppola (who died in 2024) offers thoughts about her family’s legacy of filmmaking, and the film is charmingly narrated by Diane Lane.
